paragraphs.text: Many students think the secret to good grades is studying for hours without a break. ____ Researchers call this the spacing effect, and it works for almost every subject.

Here is a simple plan. After class, spend fifteen minutes reviewing the main points. Then wait a day before you look at them again. ____ Each review can then be shorter than the one before, because the material feels more familiar.
Sleep matters as well. ____ While you rest, your brain quietly sorts and stores what you learned during the day.

Finally, test yourself instead of simply rereading. Close the book and write down everything you remember. ____ That little struggle is exactly what makes memory stronger. The next time homework piles up, do not reach for another energy drink. ____ Divide the work into small pieces, space them out, and protect your sleep.

Last September, our biology teacher, Ms. Chen, turned a piece of waste ground behind the school into a garden. At first, only a few students joined the project. ____ Soon, however, more than sixty names were on the watering list, and teachers began bringing their classes outside.

Each class took care of its own bed. We planted lettuce, tomatoes and sunflowers, and kept a diary of their growth. ____ When the first tomatoes turned red, we carried them to the school kitchen, and the cook made a salad for the whole grade.

The garden also changed how we study. Facts from the textbook became things we could touch and taste. ____ In geography we measured rainfall and drew charts of it; in English we wrote instructions for planting. ____ One classmate who hardly ever spoke in class turned out to be an insect expert, and we listened to him as carefully as we listen to our teachers.

In June we held a small harvest festival beside the flower beds. Parents were invited, and the money from selling vegetables went to the village school library. ____ Ms. Chen says the garden will double in size next autumn, and this time nobody doubts it.
Every night, whether you remember it or not, your brain tells stories. Most dreams fade within minutes of waking, yet they return night after night. ____ Recent studies now offer some clues.

One strong idea links dreams to learning. In an experiment, students who learned a new computer game in the morning improved faster that week if they had dreamed about it. ____ It seems the sleeping brain replays new skills, the way a coach reviews yesterday's match.

Dreams also work with feelings. Volunteers who watched an emotional film before bed showed calmer reactions to it the next morning, and their brain scans revealed why: during dreams, the emotion centres lit up again and again, each time with less intensity. ____ Night after night, this gentle repetition seems to take the sting out of painful memories.

Not every dream carries a deep message, though. Many are strange mixtures of recent events, put together in silly combinations. ____ A student who spent the day packing for a trip might dream of a school building made of suitcases. To some researchers, such dreams are simply the brain sorting through the day's leftovers.

Whatever dreams are finally shown to be, they are not useless accidents. ____ So the next time you wake with a strange story in your head, treat it with respect: it may be a small report on how your brain cared for you overnight.

Every Saturday morning, fourteen-year-old Lin Tao rides his bike to the small railway station in town. He is not there to travel. ____ For two years, he has spent the morning reading news aloud to older passengers whose eyes are weak.
It started with one man. Grandpa Wang used to sit alone, holding a paper very close to his eyes. ____ Lin Tao offered to read the sports page, and soon other passengers gathered around to listen.

Now about ten people join the reading circle each week. Lin Tao chooses stories about health, weather and local news. ____ 'He reads slowly and clearly, and repeats anything we miss,' says Grandpa Wang with a proud smile.
Reading aloud has also changed Lin Tao. ____ His teacher says his writing is full of lively details now, and his confidence in class has grown as well.
Some passengers bring him eggs or home-grown vegetables, which he politely shares with the listeners. ____ Lin Tao says he will continue until he leaves town for senior high school.
When insects attack a plant, the plant does not stay silent. ____ Scientists discovered that the injured plant sends chemicals into the air, warning its neighbours of danger.

In one classic experiment, researchers put two groups of plants in the same room and let caterpillars eat the leaves of one group. ____ Days later, however, those healthy plants had produced a bitter substance that made their leaves hard to digest.

The chemical message works like a school bell. ____ As soon as a neighbouring plant 'smells' the warning in the air, it begins producing its own bitter chemicals, even though no insect has touched it yet. This early preparation explains why some fields suffer less damage during insect outbreaks than others.

Farmers are now testing how to use this natural system. Some spray a safe chemical that imitates the warning signal, and the whole field prepares itself for attack. ____ In the future, crops may be protected not by stronger poisons but by better communication.

There is still much to learn. Plants have no ears or eyes, yet they clearly sense the world around them. ____ The quiet conversations in a field remind us that even the stillness of nature is full of activity.
Walking to school is one of the easiest ways to stay healthy. It costs nothing, needs no equipment, and takes only a few minutes more than the bus.
A short walk in the morning wakes up the brain. Scientists found that children who walk to school concentrate better in their first lessons than those who ride in a car.
Walking is also a social time. Walking with a friend or a classmate gives you a few quiet minutes to talk before the busy day begins.
Finally, walking helps the city. Fewer cars near the school gate mean cleaner air and safer streets for everyone.
Start with two or three days a week, and see how you feel after a month.
